headings.title: Introduction and Importance of Healthcare Waste Management
headings.content: Healthcare waste management encompasses all the steps involved in gathering, handling, sorting, storing, transporting, and treating waste generated within medical facilities. Poor disposal practices endanger healthcare workers, waste handlers, patients, and the surrounding community through accidental needle sticks, toxic exposures, and environmental contamination. In busy clinical settings across Nigeria, from primary health centres to tertiary teaching hospitals, proper segregation at the point of origin remains the single most effective safeguard against public health hazards.

headings.title: General (Non-Hazardous) Healthcare Waste
headings.content:
Non-hazardous waste constitutes the vast majority—roughly 75 to 90 percent—of total materials discarded by healthcare facilities. This stream resembles municipal domestic garbage and poses no special biological, chemical, or radioactive threat.

- **Food remnants**: Kitchen waste and leftover meals from patient wards.
- **Office supplies**: Paper, cardboard, packaging materials, and plastic bottles.
- **Uncontaminated linen**: Bedding and garments washed without exposure to infectious body fluids.

headings.title: Hazardous Infectious and Pathological Waste
headings.content: Infectious waste contains pathogens in sufficient concentration or quantity to cause disease in susceptible hosts. This category includes items contaminated with blood and other body fluids, laboratory cultures, and isolation ward materials. Pathological waste consists of recognizable human tissues, organs, body parts, and recognizable fetuses. Both types require immediate containment in leak-proof, biohazard-marked containers and often necessitate high-temperature incineration to completely destroy infectious agents before final disposal.

headings.title: Sharps Waste and Associated Risks
headings.content:
Sharps are items capable of puncturing or cutting skin, representing a severe occupational hazard due to their potential to transmit bloodborne infections like Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV. 

| Item Type | Clinical Example | Primary Risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Needles | Hypodermic needles, suture needles | Puncture wounds, bloodborne virus transfer |
| Blades | Scalpel blades, surgical razors | Lacerations, tissue damage |
| Glassware | Broken ampoules, capillary tubes | Cuts, direct chemical or germ entry |

All sharps must be dropped directly into puncture-resistant safety boxes without recapping.

headings.title: Pharmaceutical, Chemical, and Genotoxic Waste
headings.content: Pharmaceutical waste includes expired, unused, spilled, or contaminated drugs, vaccines, and sera. Chemical waste consists of discarded solid, liquid, and gaseous chemicals used in diagnostic procedures, cleaning, and housekeeping. Genotoxic waste is highly hazardous and includes cytotoxic drugs used in cancer treatment, along with mutagenic and teratogenic chemicals. These substances can cause severe poisoning, genetic mutations, or fetal abnormalities if allowed to leach into local water sources or soil.

headings.title: Radioactive and Specialized Waste Categories
headings.content: Radioactive waste comprises solid, liquid, and gaseous materials contaminated with radionuclides generated from in vitro analysis of body tissue and fluid, tumor localization, and radiotherapy treatments. This category requires strict regulatory control, as radiation exposure poses profound health risks. Materials must be stored in specialized containers until their radioactivity decays to safe background levels, after which they may be handled according to their chemical or physical properties.

headings.title: Color-Coding and Segregation Protocols in Nigerian Health Facilities
headings.content: Standardized color-coding ensures rapid identification and appropriate handling of different waste categories across healthcare facilities in Nigeria. Black or brown bins typically receive non-hazardous municipal waste. Yellow bins with biohazard symbols hold infectious and pathological items. Puncture-proof safety boxes, often yellow or labeled clearly, collect sharps. Chemical and pharmaceutical wastes go into designated leak-proof containers. Strict adherence to these protocols protects sanitation workers and prevents illegal scavenging at waste dump sites.
